Talented employees who feel trapped
often leave their companies to find new
challenges elsewhere.
The drive to defend. We all
naturally defend ourselves, our
property, our family and friends and
our ideas and beliefs against external
threats. This drive is rooted in the
basic fight-or-flight response common
to most animals. In humans, it
manifests itself not just as aggressive
or defensive behavior, but also as a
quest to create institutions that
promote justice and that allow people
to express their own thoughts and
beliefs. The drive to defend tells us a
lot about people’s resistance to change;
it's one reason employees can be
distressed by the prospect of their
company being taken over, even if the
deal represents the only hope for an
organization's survival.
So what actions can managers take
to satisfy the four drives and, thereby,
increase their employees’ overall
motivation? We recently completed
two major studies to evaluate the
importance of these drives in terms of
employee motivation. In one, we
Surveyed 385 employees of two global
businesses. In the other, we surveyed
employees from 300 successful local
companies. To define overall
motivation, we focused on four
commonly measured workplace
indicators: effort, satisfaction,
commitment and intention to quit.

drives influence some motivational
more than others. Fulfilling
the drive to bond has the greatest
